extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, lawyers, judges, law students, and inventors interested in U.S. patent law (mid-19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the legal standards for what is patentable in the United States and the procedural and substantive requirements for patents, specifications, prosecution, assignment, infringement, and remedies. Aims to guide practitioners and courts in evaluating patent validity and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability — new and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of a patent must be new and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work repeatedly states novelty and utility are statutory requisites; invention must be substantially new and beneficial to society. Utility is a test of invention in American law; the degree of utility is not material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject-matter includes machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, processes (modes), and improvements thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise classifies what may be a patentable subject and distinguishes these categories (machine, manufacture, composition, process). It notes limits such as mere theories, abstract principles, or pure sciences not being patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (anticipation) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is a statutory requisite; prior public use, sale, or prior description in a public work can destroy novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty implies more than trivial differences; slight evidence of novelty may be sufficient, but prior public use/publication/printed work/foreign patents inconsistent with novelty can defeat it. The treatise discusses modes of proving novelty and that there are two issues concerning novelty in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (usefulness) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be useful; utility is a test of invention and must relate to the whole invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of utility affects the validity and remedies; but the degree of utility is immaterial. Patent must be beneficial to society; failure of utility can render patent void or affect damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle vs application — abstract principle not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle in the abstract (theory) is not patentable; an application or embodiment of a principle may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise warns that an abstract principle (elementary principle, science, mere purpose) is not patentable; the patentable subject is the application of such principle in matter (a process, machine, manufacture, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode / disclosure of how to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must state the best mode of producing the effect and disclose enough that others of ordinary skill can practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications should be addressed to persons of competent skill, state the best mode, disclose every thing essential, and not require undue experimentation. Failure to disclose best mode or essential details can render a patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications must agree with the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must agree with the letters-patent; repugnancy between them has legal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications and drawings are construed together with the patent. Courts construe specifications liberally but require that the patent not claim more than described; contradictions or repugnancies are material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims / patent scope must not exceed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be more extensive than the invention; it should contain no more than is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are construed with the specification; a patent that attempts to cover distinct inventions or to be broader than described is invalid to that extent. The patent relates back to date of invention but is limited to what was actually invented and described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity (singleness) of the subject-matter is required by statute; patents should possess unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where two distinct inventions are claimed they may violate unity; the treatise explains when several things can be embraced in one patent (improvements, related combinations) and when not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications must distinguish old from new
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications should distinguish what is old (prior art) from the new contribution of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps prevent misleading the public; specifications should describe what is old briefly and clearly show the novel features. Misleading descriptions are a common defect under English cases summarized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications must not be ambiguous or misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must not be ambiguous, mislead the public, or use terms loosely or incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous terms, omissions of necessary descriptions, incorrect drawings, or things put in to mislead are cited as major defects; such defects may render a patent invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings as part of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings annexed to the specification form part of it and should accompany specifications when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains why drawings are required and how they aid in describing the invention; incorrect drawings are a common defect and can be grounds for invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address to skilled persons; use of technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications are to be written for persons of competent skill in the art and may contain technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee need not instruct a layman; the disclosure standard is the person skilled in the art. Technical language is permissible; the specification should enable such a person to practice the invention without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of description — disclose every thing essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications should describe every thing essential to the invention but need not describe what the patentee is not claiming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some things need not be described, omissions of essential details can invalidate. Slight defects may be fatal; the description should include materials of a machine when necessary and be precise about essential elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and disclaimers allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments of specifications and disclaimers are allowed by statute in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise discusses statutory allowance for amendment, disclaimers, reissue, and the conditions under which the patentee may alter the specification or patent (e.g., surrender and reissue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode, experiments and experimental claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must state the best mode and should not require excessive experiments; in some cases experiments may be required to prove operability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must describe the best-known mode; while the specification should not impose undue experimental burden, some practical experimentation in follow-up disclosure may be necessary in complex chemical or experimental arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use and sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior public use or sale before the statutory period destroys the right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise analyzes what constitutes public use, how to prove it, and its effects; prior use inconsistent with secrecy or within statutory bar prevents patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication / prior description
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior description in a public printed work is inconsistent with novelty and can defeat patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine of anticipation by printed publication is discussed (what counts as a public work) and how foreign publications or prior descriptions affect U.S. patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patents and prior foreign disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior foreign patents or disclosures may be inconsistent with novelty in the U.S. under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise notes how foreign patents relate to novelty and U.S. patenting, when they prevent a U.S. patent, and how prior foreign public use or description is treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious substitution / mere substitution not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere substitution of one known material or method for another obvious to a skilled person is not an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise covers the boundary between genuine invention and obvious substitutions, explaining that an obvious substitution is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of thought / non-frivolous invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention requires more than a frivolous change; a sufficient degree of thought or new application is required to constitute invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author addresses how much inventive thought is necessary, emphasizing that trivial changes do not qualify but slight evidence of novelty can sometimes suffice depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of invention and result as test
rubrics_metrics.description: The production of a new and useful result is a great test of invention; the result produced helps show sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise uses examples (steam engine, heated blast) to show that applying natural laws to produce new effects constitutes invention when it produces a tangible, useful result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to combinations and multiple inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When several things are described or several improvements claimed, the specification and patent must be construed to determine whether separate patents are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains how combinations and improvements may be treated in one patent, when several improvements can be embraced together, and when separate patents are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent construction and liberal construction of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts construe patents and specifications liberally but will not allow a patent to cover more than the invention described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation principles: specifications and patent read together, liberally construed for the patentee but limited to what is described and enabled. The court decides scope and jury may assess technical fact questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and burden in infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff bears the burden of proving infringement; patent itself is prima facie evidence of novelty but other evidentiary rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise outlines modes of proof for novelty and infringement, what evidence beyond the patent may be offered, and how courts allocate issues of law and fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — law and equity (damages and injunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies for infringement include actions at law for damages and equitable relief (injunctions) to restrain infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book discusses practice and principles for obtaining damages, rules for calculating damages, and when injunctions/quia timet bills are appropriate; also the interplay between law and equity remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking requirement and penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees are required to mark patented articles offered for sale; failure or false marking entails penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains the statutory marking requirements, the effect of marking on remedies, and penalties recoverable for false marking or failure to mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering applications and priority of inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: When two applicants claim the same invention, interfering applications procedures determine entitlement to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book discusses caveats, petitions, oaths, and how the Patent Office and courts decide priority and resolve interfering applications, including relevant dates and evidence of conception and reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath, petition, and formal patent-office requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant must file a petition, take an oath or affirmation, and pay fees; certain formalities (signatures of Secretary of State and Commissioner) are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise details the form of the oath, when affirmation suffices, irregularities and cures, and other procedural Patent Office requirements (filing, caveats, fees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Models and exhibits to the Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of the invention may be required to be furnished and are classified by the Commissioner; duplicates and compensation for models governed by rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses when models should be exhibited to the public and Patent Office, how models are handled, classification, and compensation in special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments, licenses, and recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents may be assigned or licensed; assignments should be recorded and recording can be proven in actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains transmission of interest, recording of assignments, effects on rights and enforcement, and proof of assignment in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal, extension, surrender and reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory rules govern renewal/extension of patents and the surrender and issuance of new patents (reissue) under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise describes the instances when renewal or extension is allowed, rules for surrendering a patent and obtaining a new one, and the time frames involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officials and conflict of interest restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Office officers (Commissioner, examiners, clerks, machinist, draughtsman, messenger, etc.) have duties, prescribed compensation and are disqualified from taking interest in patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that officers must make oaths, lists positions and functions, and notes restrictions on taking proprietary interests in patents to avoid conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence rules regarding witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain witnesses (users, patentees who sold machines, licensees) are competent and rules govern who is incompetent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise provides discussion about witness competency and common evidentiary issues arising in patent litigation (e.g., whether a patentee who has assigned interest can testify).
